intro: To open an Excel file in Numbers on Mac, drag the .xlsx file onto the Numbers icon in the Dock or in Applications. Or open Numbers, choose File > Open, select the file, and click Open.
tldr: Drag the Excel file onto the Numbers icon in the Dock or in Applications.
Or open Numbers, choose File > Open, pick the file, and click Open.
Control-click the file in Finder, then choose Open With > Numbers.
Numbers 15.4.2 needs macOS 26.0 or later. Update it in the Mac App Store first.
Check formulas, charts, and formatting after the file opens. Some Excel features do not carry over.

blocks.text: Open the file from inside Numbers with File > Open

This is the most direct route. It works whether or not Excel is installed on your Mac. Open Numbers first, then use the menu bar at the top of the screen. Make sure Numbers is the active app, or the menu will show another program's commands.

When the Open dialog appears, it looks like a normal Finder window. Go to the folder that holds your workbook, such as Downloads or Documents. Select the file and click Open. Numbers reads the workbook and makes a new Numbers spreadsheet from it.
Drag the Excel file onto the Numbers icon

Apple's guide suggests dragging for Excel files, and the reason is simple. Double-clicking an Excel file in Finder opens Microsoft Excel when Excel is installed. A drag sends the file to Numbers instead. Drop it on the Numbers icon in the Dock or in the Applications folder.

Dragging also suits a file you just downloaded. Keep a Finder window open beside the Dock. Point at the workbook, hold the mouse button, and move it over the Numbers icon. Let go when the pointer sits on the icon.

blocks.title: Numbers not in the Dock?
blocks.text: Drag the file onto Numbers in Applications instead. In Finder, choose Go > Applications, then find Numbers in the list.
Control-click the file and choose Open With

Control-click works well when you want Numbers for one file and nothing else changes. Hold Control and click the Excel file. You can also right-click it with a mouse or trackpad. Hover over Open With, then choose Numbers from the list.
If Numbers is missing from that list, it may be out of date or not installed. Check the Mac App Store, install the latest Numbers, and try again.
You can also make Numbers the default for every .xlsx file. Select the file in Finder and press ⌘ I to open Get Info. Expand Open with, choose Numbers, and click Change All.

blocks.title: Change All affects every file
blocks.text: After this, every .xlsx file on your Mac opens in Numbers by double-click. Someone else using the Mac may not expect that. To switch back, repeat Get Info and choose Microsoft Excel.
Pick the method that fits the job
Each method ends in the same place, a Numbers spreadsheet. The difference is where you start. The table below shows which method suits common situations.

blocks.text: If Numbers is already open and you need a file from another folder, File > Open keeps you in the app. If you are sorting files in Finder anyway, dragging is faster.
Reopen a workbook from File > Open Recent

After the first import, you may need the workbook again. Go to File > Open Recent in Numbers. Apple's guide says this list shows up to the last ten spreadsheets. Pick the one you need, and it opens without a file browser.

Open Recent tracks spreadsheets you have opened in Numbers. The copy you edit in Numbers is what appears there, not the original Excel file. Decide early which file is your master, so you do not edit two versions by accident.
Open several Excel workbooks in tabs

If you work from three or four workbooks at once, separate windows pile up fast. Numbers can open each file as a tab in one window instead. Go to System Settings > Desktop & Dock, open the Windows section, and turn on Prefer tabs when opening documents.

The setting applies to every app that supports tabs, not only Numbers. Once it is on, open each workbook with one of the methods above. Each file lands in a tab in the same window, so you can switch between them without hunting through the Dock.

Tabs help when you compare the original Excel file with the Numbers copy you are building. Keep the Excel file in one tab and the Numbers copy in another. Then check the totals side by side, one sheet at a time.
Check the sheet after it opens

Numbers does its best with Excel files, but the result is not always an exact copy. Macworld's guide says formatting may change, especially charts. It also advises checking that formulas are intact. The simpler the spreadsheet, the closer the match.
Start with the cells that matter most. Double-click a formula cell to read its formula. Compare the result with the Excel file. If totals differ, look for a function that Numbers handles differently.

items: Formulas: compare totals and key results with the Excel original.
Charts: confirm each chart points at the right table and sits on the right sheet.
Images and text: check that they did not shift during import.
Fonts: choose Format > Font > Replace Fonts for any font your Mac does not have.
Conditional formatting: rules do not transfer, so set them up again if you need them.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make after opening Excel in Numbers
The most common mistake is editing the Numbers copy and forgetting the Excel file. A colleague then receives the old Excel version. Pick one master file and tell the team which one it is.
Another mistake is trusting the first look. A sheet can appear fine while one formula on another tab is wrong. Scroll through each tab and spot-check key figures against the original.
People also copy cells by hand when they need Excel again. Copying is slow and easy to get wrong. File > Export To > Excel handles the whole workbook in one step.
What Numbers does not carry over from Excel
Numbers is not a copy of Excel. It has about 250 functions. Excel has more than 450, according to How-To Geek. Check any function that is unusual in your file, since it may not exist in Numbers.

Macros and VBA code do not run in Numbers. Slicers and timelines are not supported. Conditional formatting rules are not transferred. Aptos Narrow does not work natively in Numbers, so text set in that font needs another font.
How-To Geek also notes that charts and images can end up in the wrong places after import. Macworld makes the same point about charts. Plan time to look at every sheet before you rely on the result.
Size limits for large Excel workbooks
Excel worksheets hold up to 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns, according to Microsoft. Each cell can contain up to 32,767 characters. Those limits describe Excel, not Numbers.

Datablist, a third-party guide, states that Numbers supports up to 1,000,000 rows per table. It does not name a Numbers or macOS version, so treat the figure as a rough guide. If your sheet approaches that size, split it before you import.
Large files also open more slowly and scroll less smoothly. Splitting one sheet into several smaller tables keeps each part easier to check.
Open Excel files in Numbers on iCloud.com

You can skip the Mac app entirely. Sign in to iCloud.com, open Numbers, and drag the file into the browser window. You can also click Upload, select the file, and click Upload again. Then double-click the file to open it.

Apple's iCloud page lists XLSX among the formats Numbers supports. It does not list .xls. Macworld's steps say .xls works in the Mac app, so results can vary. If an .xls file fails, save a copy as .xlsx in Excel and upload that instead.
Fix a file that will not open in Numbers

A dimmed file in the Open dialog means Numbers cannot open it. Apple's guide says to update Numbers from the Mac App Store and check the file format. Run those two checks before you try anything else.

If Excel opens when you expected Numbers, the default app is set to Excel. Get Info fixes that. Microsoft's support answer for a similar problem uses the same Change All step, so the steps carry over.
Save your work and export back to Excel
Numbers saves its own format. Press ⌘ S or choose File > Save to keep your changes. Close the spreadsheet with ⌘ W when you finish, as Apple's guide describes.

To send the workbook back to Excel, choose File > Export To > Excel. Apple's steps let you choose a worksheet for each table or for each sheet. You can also add an optional summary worksheet and a password.
Apple's steps finish with Save, then Where > Export. Check the destination before you confirm, so the file lands where your team looks for it.

Once the sheet is open, you may want to tidy it. See [How to sort a table in Numbers on Mac by column, step by step](/how-to/sort-a-table-by-column-in-numbers) and [How to filter a table in Numbers on Mac: filter table rows step by step](/how-to/filter-table-rows-in-numbers).
Who should open Excel files in Numbers

Numbers suits people who need to view, check, or lightly edit a workbook. It also suits a team that works on Macs and wants a Numbers file. Keep the Excel file as the master if the workbook uses macros, slicers, or many Excel-only functions.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to open an Excel file in Numbers?
faq.answer: Apple's Numbers pages do not list a shortcut for importing an Excel file. The reliable routes are File > Open, dragging the file onto the Numbers icon, and Control-click > Open With > Numbers. Use ⌘ W to close the spreadsheet when you finish.

faq.question: Do I need Excel installed to open the file in Numbers?
faq.answer: No. Numbers opens the file on its own. Excel only matters for double-clicking, because a double-click on an Excel file opens Excel when Excel is installed. That is why dragging is the safer habit.

faq.question: Can Numbers open .xls files as well as .xlsx?
faq.answer: Macworld's steps say the method works with both .xlsx and .xls. Apple's iCloud page lists XLSX but not XLS. If an older .xls file fails, save a copy as .xlsx in Excel and try again.

faq.question: Will my formulas still work after I open the file?
faq.answer: Many will, but not all. Numbers has about 250 functions, against more than 450 in Excel. Check key results against the Excel file, and replace any function that Numbers does not have.

faq.question: What is the largest Excel file Numbers can open?
faq.answer: Excel allows 1,048,576 rows per worksheet. Datablist, a third-party guide, says Numbers supports up to 1,000,000 rows per table. Split very large sheets before you import them.

faq.question: Why does Numbers create a new document from my Excel file?
faq.answer: Numbers imports the workbook into its own format. Edits you make in Numbers stay in the Numbers copy. Keep the original Excel file if other people still need it.

faq.question: Can I make Numbers the default app for Excel files?
faq.answer: Yes, with Get Info. Select the file in Finder, choose File > Get Info, open Open with, select Numbers, and click Change All. Excel stops opening .xlsx files by double-click until you change it back.

task: Open an Excel file in Numbers on Mac
requirements: A Mac running macOS 26.0 or later for Numbers 15.4.2
Numbers installed from the Mac App Store
The Excel workbook, ideally saved as .xlsx
Finder access to the folder that holds the file

steps.name: Update Numbers
steps.text: Open the Mac App Store and check the Updates section. Numbers 15.4.2 is the current version, and it needs macOS 26.0 or later. An older macOS cannot run this version.
steps.tip: If Numbers is not listed under Updates, it is already current.

steps.name: Open Numbers
steps.text: Open Numbers from Applications, Launchpad, or Spotlight. With Spotlight, press ⌘ Space, type Numbers, and press Return.

steps.name: Open the File menu
steps.text: With Numbers active, go to the menu bar and choose File > Open. The File menu only shows Numbers commands while Numbers is the front app.
steps.tip: Apple's guide does not list a shortcut for this command. Use the menu if a shortcut does nothing.

steps.name: Choose the Excel file
steps.text: In the Open dialog, go to the folder that holds your workbook. Select the file. Excel's default format is .xlsx, so most workbooks you receive end that way.
steps.tip: A dimmed file means Numbers cannot open it. Check the format and update Numbers.

steps.name: Click Open
steps.text: Click Open in the dialog. Numbers reads the workbook and creates a new Numbers spreadsheet from it. Your original Excel file stays as it was.
steps.tip: Keep the Excel file somewhere safe as your original copy.

steps.name: Check every sheet
steps.text: Click through each sheet tab in the window. Make sure each table and chart came across. Large or complicated workbooks take longer to load.

steps.name: Check formulas and charts
steps.text: Double-click a few formula cells and compare the totals with the Excel file. Confirm each chart points at the right data. Macworld advises checking that formulas are intact after import.
steps.tip: Keep the Excel file open in another window while you compare.

steps.name: Save the Numbers copy
steps.text: Press ⌘ S or choose File > Save. The Numbers version is now your working copy. Close the spreadsheet with ⌘ W when you finish.

steps.name: Export back to Excel when needed
steps.text: To send the workbook back to Excel, choose File > Export To > Excel. Pick a worksheet for each table or for each sheet. Set a password if you need one, then finish with Save and Where > Export.
steps.tip: Check the destination folder before you confirm the export.

troubleshooting.problem: The Excel file is dimmed in the Open dialog
troubleshooting.fix: Numbers cannot open a dimmed file. Update Numbers from the Mac App Store, confirm the file is in a format Numbers reads, then try again.

troubleshooting.problem: Double-clicking opens Excel instead of Numbers
troubleshooting.fix: Drag the file onto the Numbers icon, or use Control-click > Open With > Numbers. To make Numbers the default, use Get Info > Open with > Numbers > Change All.

troubleshooting.problem: Macros or VBA buttons do nothing
troubleshooting.fix: Numbers does not run macros or VBA code. Keep the macro workbook in Excel, or rebuild the logic with Numbers formulas.

troubleshooting.problem: Charts or images are in the wrong place
troubleshooting.fix: Drag each object back into position. Charts and images can move during import, so check every sheet before you share it.

troubleshooting.problem: Conditional formatting or slicers are missing
troubleshooting.fix: Numbers does not carry over conditional formatting rules or slicers. Note what the rules did in Excel and set them up again in Numbers by hand.

troubleshooting.problem: Text appears in a different font
troubleshooting.fix: Choose Format > Font > Replace Fonts to swap a font your Mac does not have. Aptos Narrow does not work natively in Numbers, so pick another font for that text.
